title: Northwest Airlines 705
summary: The Boeing 720 departed Miami and encountered a severe thunderstorm shortly after takeoff. The aircraft encountered a severe updraft that caused a sudden nose-down maneuver, which pilots likely corrected with a pitch-up input. The aircraft entered an uncontrolled climb that exceeded structural limits, causing the aircraft to break up in flight.
probable_cause: Aircraft entered severe turbulence and updrafts in a thunderstorm shortly after takeoff that exceeded the aircraft's structural design limits, causing in-flight breakup.

factors.evidence: Severe thunderstorm with moderate to heavy turbulence and severe updrafts shortly after takeoff
Aircraft encountered severe updraft causing uncontrolled pitch-up and rate of climb gradually increasing to approximately 9000 ft/min
Aircraft broke up in midair due to forces exceeding structural limits

events.text: Aircraft cleared to climb to flight level 250 from 5000 ft, entered area with moderate to heavy turbulence
Aircraft control transferred to Miami ARTCC, entered severe updraft
Severe updraft caused nose-down maneuver followed by pilot pitch-up, aircraft altitude increased with rate of climb reaching approximately 9000 ft/min
Aircraft broke up in midair over Florida Everglades, wreckage crashed into swamp

notes: Text truncated, probable cause section not included, details of structural failure mechanism inferred from description of break-up

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 293
summary: A Douglas DC-7C chartered by the Military Air Transport Service to carry 95 servicemen and their families from Washington state to Alaska crashed into the sea off the coast of Alaska on June 3, 1963. The last radio contact was at 10:06 a.m. when the crew requested a flight level change, and floating debris was discovered 182.5 miles WSW of Annette Island. All 101 people aboard perished.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed into the sea with all occupants killed and minimal wreckage recovered

events.text: Flight 293 departed McChord Air Force Base at 07:52 Pacific Standard Time carrying 95 servicemen and their families
At 10:06 the crew requested a change of flight level; this was the last radio contact with the aircraft
A search for the aircraft was begun after no contact for more than an hour
Floating debris including life vests still in plastic containers and deformed seat frames were found 182.5 miles WSW of Annette Island

notes: Exact cause could not be determined due to wreckage depth (8000 feet); only structural failure or loss of control inferred from total casualties

title: Swissair 306
summary: Flight 306 took off from Zurich in dense fog and reached 2700 meters altitude four minutes after takeoff. A white trail of smoke was observed from the left side of the aircraft, followed by a long flame from the left wing. The aircraft entered a gentle left turn and began descending more steeply into a final dive. A Mayday was issued and the aircraft crashed near Dürrenäsch. The accident resulted from overheated aircraft brakes during taxiing through fog at full engine power, causing magnesium wheels to burst.
probable_cause: Aircraft brakes overheated from application of full engine power during taxiing to disperse fog. Magnesium wheels burst, with one bursting on the runway before departure. When landing gear retracted after takeoff, hydraulic lines in the gear bay were damaged by burst wheel rim fragments. Spilled hydraulic fluid ignited when contacting overheated landing gear rims, causing fire in the gear bay that spread to the wing. The resulting electrical problems and structural damage led to loss of control.

factors.evidence: Application of full engine power during taxiing in fog to disperse weather was unusual procedure
Magnesium wheels and vulnerable hydraulic line routing in landing gear bay susceptible to damage from wheel burst fragments
Hydraulic lines in gear bay damaged when wheel rims burst during gear retraction; hydraulic fluid loss
Spilled hydraulic fluid ignited when contacting hot landing gear rims; fire damaged gear bay and wing structure
Aircraft entered uncontrolled descent with left wing engulfed in flame; left engine shutdown unknown whether crew or fire-caused

events.text: Aircraft took off from runway 34 after taxi involving high engine power to disperse dense fog; brakes applied during this taxi
White smoke trail observed coming from left side of aircraft as it climbed; long flame erupted from left wing
Aircraft reached approximately 2700 meters, began gentle left turn then descended more steeply, entered final steep dive
Aircraft in final steep dive when Mayday message was issued as fire spread through wing structure
Aircraft crashed into ground on outskirts of Dürrenäsch approximately 35 kilometers from Zurich Airport

notes: probable cause clearly stated in investigation
sequence of fire and loss of control well documented

title: Trans-Canada Air Lines 831
summary: Trans-Canada Air Lines Flight 831, a Douglas DC-8 departing Montreal on 29 November 1963 in poor weather, deviated from expected flight path about five minutes after takeoff and began a quick descent. At 6:33 p.m., the jet struck the ground at an estimated 470 mph while descending at approximately 55 degrees. The investigation could not determine the exact cause but pointed to problems in the jet's pitch trim system.
probable_cause: The investigation could not determine the exact cause of the accident, though problems in the aircraft's pitch trim system were identified as a possible factor.

factors.evidence: the aircraft deviated from its expected flight path and began a quick descent
it pointed to problems in the jet's pitch trim system as a possibility
the investigation was unable to determine the exact cause due to lack of flight data recorders
About five minutes after takeoff in poor weather conditions, the aircraft deviated and crashed

events.text: At 6:28 p.m., the DC-8 began its takeoff roll on Dorval airport's Runway 06R.
The crew reported back when they reached 3000 ft and were given clearance for a left turn.
Thereafter, the aircraft deviated from its expected flight path and began a quick descent.
At about 6:33 p.m., the jet struck the ground at an estimated 470 mph while descending at about a 55-degree angle.
The aircraft plunged into a soggy field in Sainte-Therese, Quebec.

notes: Investigation could not determine exact cause due to missing flight recorders

title: Pan Am 214
summary: The Boeing 707 was holding in a thunderstorm with heavy rain and lightning when a lightning strike ignited flammable fuel vapor in the left wing fuel tank, causing an explosion that destroyed the wing. The aircraft went out of control and crashed in flames in a cornfield.
probable_cause: Lightning strike ignited fuel vapor in the left wing fuel tank, causing an explosion that destroyed the wing. The exact manner of ignition could not be determined but led to increased awareness of aircraft vulnerability to lightning damage.

factors.evidence: Heavy rain, strong winds up to 50 mph, frequent lightning in holding pattern
Lightning strike probably ignited fuel vapor in one of the aircraft's fuel tanks, causing an explosion
Explosion destroyed the left wing, aircraft went out of control
Aircraft exploded and crashed in flames, wreckage burned in intense fires lasting more than four hours

events.text: Controller informed pilots that airport was experiencing thunderstorms, strong winds and turbulence, asked if they wanted to hold or proceed
Aircraft held at 5000 ft in holding pattern with frequent lightning and heavy rain, gusts up to 50 mph
Lightning struck the aircraft, igniting fuel vapor in the left wing tank, causing an explosion
Pilots transmitted final message: 'Mayday mayday mayday, Clipper 214 out of control. Here we go'
Aircraft crashed in flames in a cornfield in Cecil County, Maryland near Elkton, destroying the fuselage and spreading burning jet fuel across wide area
